# Vector affine costs: exact work identities and a hidden positive fiber

This note tests whether affine costs can extend the scalar mixed-plus-own
potential into a selector covering the original mixed set. The valid
identities retain affine work. A complete actual convex example shows
that neither base costs nor full-point costs expose all positive fibers
or their deep regions, even under strict exclusion of a heavy fiber.
No OC counterexample or impossibility of every vector charging method
is asserted.

## 1. Actual sources and vector exchange

Work with finitely many positive d-dimensional convex fibers, d>=1,
and their original mixed measure mu. Let D(Y) be raw mixed depth,
f(Y) ordinary raw own-fiber depth, and F(Y)=f(Y)^(1/d). These are the
same quantities, with attainment and continuity, as in
`candidate 8280d34e5808dfad`.
Choose either p(Y)=z (base costs) or p(Y)=Y (full-point costs), and put

    E(lambda,b)=max_(Y in S)[D(Y)+lambda F(Y)+b.p(Y)],
    theta=(lambda,b),   w(Y)=(F(Y),p(Y)),   lambda>=0.

Compactness gives an actual maximizing source for every parameter.
Full-point costs can select fiber-boundary sources, so no positive-own
section assertion is made without that separate hypothesis. Base costs
preserve interior maximization within any selected positive fiber.
The zero measured fibers may first be removed by the archived positive-
fiber hull reduction when a selection theorem needs that property.

For selected sources Y_i at theta_i, define delta w=w(Y1)-w(Y0) and
A=D(Y0)-D(Y1). The two maximizing comparisons give exactly

    theta0.delta w <= A <= theta1.delta w,               (1)
    (theta1-theta0).delta w >=0.                         (2)

Thus actual depth need not decrease as the vector parameter changes.
For example the scalar nonnegative-work term lambda delta F is replaced
by lambda delta F+b.delta p at a tied parameter. Discarding the affine
term in (1) is invalid.

Along an affine parameter path theta(t)=theta0+t v, let

    G(t)=v.w(Y_t),   R(t)=D(Y_t)+theta0.w(Y_t),

where Y_t maximizes the objective and G(t) is the largest active slope.
The scalar envelope argument applies verbatim to R+tG: G is bounded,
monotone, and right-continuous, and

    R(a)-R(b)=integral_(a,b] t dG(t).                    (3)

In terms of ACTUAL depth, rather than the adjusted intercept, this is

    D(Y_a)-D(Y_b)
      =integral_(a,b] t dG(t)
           +theta0.[w(Y_b)-w(Y_a)].                    (4)

The last term is indispensable. Formula (3) concerns values of actual
maximizers, with the maximum-slope convention; no measurable source
path is needed. It follows by the finite-partition exchange proof used
for the scalar envelope. Formula (4) is its exact algebraic rearrangement.

## 2. Same-cost midpoint charges still use actual depth order

Let two sources tie at a common theta=(lambda,b), lambda>0. Suppose
both are interior to positive fibers and their midpoint Ym is actual.
Relabel so that D0>=D1 and put A=D0-D1. Own-root concavity supplies
Delta=F(Ym)-(F0+F1)/2>=0, while affine p gives

    D(Ym)<= (D0+D1)/2-lambda Delta.                     (5)

If A>0, every actual depth-attaining nonvertical cap H={L>=0}
through Ym excludes Y0 and contains Y1 strictly. The same argument
as for the scalar potential proves this directly from D(Ym)<D0.
Writing s=L(Y1)>0, the actual slab T=mu{0<=L<s} is positive and

    T+lambda Delta <=A/2,
    A=lambda(F1-F0)+b.[p(Y1)-p(Y0)].                    (6)

Unlike scalar same-parameter selection, F1-F0 need not be positive.
If A=0, depth quasiconcavity and (5) force Delta=0 and D(Ym)=D0;
positive own-fiber slabs force both endpoints onto every critical
midpoint plane. These are actual geometric statements. They provide
no automatic orientation of a multi-parameter chain by its parameters.

For two different parameter vectors, follow their straight joining
segment. Put B0=(theta1-theta0).delta w. If B0>0, the two endpoint
objective lines meet at

    t*=[A-theta0.delta w]/B0 in [0,1].

At theta*=theta0+t*(theta1-theta0), let B be the envelope height above
their common value. Convexity yields

    0<=B<=t*(1-t*) B0<=B0/4.                            (7)

For an actual midpoint cap containing endpoint e, its actual slab T_e
therefore satisfies

    T_e+lambda* Delta
       <=(D_(1-e)-D_e)/2+B<=|A|/2+B.                  (8)

Here lambda* is the lambda-coordinate of theta*. In contrast to (6),
the endpoint of smaller D is not asserted to face every cap: the gap B
can prevent that conclusion. Equations (1), (4), and (8) are the exact
work and gap corrections required by vector costs.

## 3. A strict-noheavy actual simplex chain

Let T be any planar simplex of area one, with a vertex at the origin;
for explicit coordinates take T=conv{(0,0),(2,0),(0,1)}. Define

    r(z)=(1+3z)/4,
    C={(z,x):0<=z<=5, x in r(z)T}.

This is a compact full-dimensional convex body: r is positive affine,
and the displayed family is the convex hull of its two endpoint fibers.
Its COMPLETE integer base set is {0,1,2,3,4,5}, and its actual fibers
are r_j T with r_j=(1+3j)/4. Their areas, in order, are

    (1,16,49,100,169,256)/16.

Consequently

    M=591/16,  max_j |C_j|=16 < M/2=591/32.             (9)

All fibers have positive area and no fiber is heavy at the n=1 threshold.
No arbitrary incomplete sampled base is being used.

Write Gamma=4/9 for the ordinary planar-simplex maximum depth fraction.
For x in T, homothety gives

    f_(rT)(rx)=r^2 f_T(x),   F_(rT)(rx)=r sqrt(f_T(x)).  (10)

The ordinary simplex centroid has depth Gamma, and no point has greater
own depth. This is the classical sharp simplex Grünbaum fact. The upper
bound also follows immediately by taking the vertex cap corresponding
to a largest barycentric coordinate, whose area is at most (2/3)^2.

At base zero, finite integer tilt isolates the own fiber, so D=f there.
At base one, any ordinary cap through x can be extended to an ambient
cap containing ALL of base zero and NONE of bases two through five:
write its continuous inequality u.(X-x)>=0 and take

    u.(X-x)-L(z-1)>=0

with L sufficiently large. There are finitely many bounded fibers, so
a finite such L exists. Minimizing the own direction gives the exact
upper bound

    D(1,x)<=f_T(x)+1/16.                                (11)

At every base, D is at least ordinary own depth, because a containing
ambient cap contains a through-source own-fiber cap (or the whole fiber).
These facts hold for ALL relevant directions; (11) is a certified cap
upper bound, not a numerical minimization claim.

## 4. Base one is never exposed by any base affine cost

Fix lambda>=0 and let

    h_lambda(j)=max_(x in C_j)[D(j,x)+lambda F(j,x)].

The scalar map s+lambda sqrt(s) is increasing for s>=0. Thus (11) and
the simplex own-depth maximum give

    h_lambda(1)<=Gamma+1/16+lambda sqrt(Gamma)
                 =73/144+2lambda/3.                   (12)

At base zero, exact isolation gives

    h_lambda(0)=1/36+lambda/6.                          (13)

At base two, choosing its ordinary centroid and using D>=f gives

    h_lambda(2)>=49/36+7lambda/6.                        (14)

Therefore

    [h_lambda(0)+h_lambda(2)]/2-h_lambda(1)>=3/16>0      (15)

for EVERY lambda>=0. For any real affine base cost b z, the b term at
base one is the average of its values at bases zero and two. Equation
(15) makes the objective at base one strictly less than the average of
those two base optima, hence less than at least one of them. Thus no
point of the entire positive fiber at base one is selected by ANY
base-cost vector envelope at ANY nonnegative lambda.

The dual cells for a finite maximum of affine functions partition cost
space in the usual way, but their selected base set need not contain
every original positive base. This actual example has strict no-heavy
and a uniform positive hidden-base gap, so these missing fibers cannot
be dismissed as zero-volume or degeneracy effects.

## 5. Full-point affine costs still miss a whole deep region

Now allow arbitrary affine costs b.(z,x), and take any x in T. The actual
points

    Y0=(0,x/4),   Y1=(1,x),   Y2=(2,7x/4)

satisfy Y1=(Y0+Y2)/2. By (10), their own-root values satisfy the exact
identity F(Y1)=[F(Y0)+F(Y2)]/2. The endpoint depth lower bounds and (11)
give

    [D(Y0)+D(Y2)]/2-D(Y1)
       >=(9/16)f_T(x)-1/16.                            (16)

If f_T(x)>1/9, the right side is strictly positive. The lambda F term
and EVERY full affine cost average exactly at these three actual
points. Consequently no point (1,x) with f_T(x)>1/9 can maximize the
full-point affine envelope, for any lambda>=0 and any b in R^3.
In particular the own-fiber centroid is hidden, with gap at least3/16.
Continuity and its depth4/9 show that the hidden set contains a nonempty
open planar region and has positive own-fiber area.

This is a strict obstruction to the proposed assertion that varying
full affine costs visits all original fiber regions. Passing to the
concave envelope or a barycentric combination of selected endpoint
sources fills the missing point only by averaging; that alone supplies
neither an actual selected point there nor a proof of OC. The example
does not exclude a different accounting theorem that explicitly pays
for these hidden regions; no such theorem is asserted here.
